intervals.label: IMB detector operating
intervals.quote: IMB was an 8,000 ton Cherenkov detector — a device able to spot a form of electromagnetic radiation that is used for particle identification — that operated between 1982 and 1991.

intervals.label: IMB run ended
intervals.note: Terminal event for the physics programme only; the APS designated the mine a historic site on 27 August 2024.
intervals.quote: IMB’s run ended in 1991, but its impact continues today.

name: Fairport Harbor Morton Salt Mine (IMB site)
notes: The facility record stands for the underground site in its role as the IMB host; the mine itself is a commercial salt mine that predates and outlives the experiment, and the APS release does not give a mine opening date.
Status decommissioned means the physics programme ended in 1991, not that the mine closed.

operator_text.note: The mine owner is the host, not an operator of the physics; the IMB collaboration ran the detector. The owner named in 1987 was Morton-Thiokol; the 2024 APS pages say "Morton Salt Mine". Present ownership was not checked.
operator_text.quote: The IMB detector, designed to search for proton decay, is located in the Morton-Thiokol salt mine near Fairport, Ohio
operator_text.value: Morton Salt (host salt mine; named the "Morton-Thiokol salt mine" in the 1987 IMB paper)

summary.plain: A salt mine in Ohio that, from 1982 to 1991, housed the IMB detector, an 8,000-ton tank of ultrapure water built to look for proton decay. It recorded neutrinos from supernova 1987A and was named an APS historic site in 2024.
summary.technical: Fairport Harbor Morton Salt Mine, Ohio: site of the Irvine-Michigan-Brookhaven (IMB) water Cherenkov detector, the first kiloton-scale nucleon-decay detector, 1982-1991, at 1570 m.w.e.
